I've gathered substantial material from the sources I could reach. Let me now compile the verse-by-verse notes. I'll note gaps where I couldn't access certain traditions.

## Micah 1 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1 — The Superscription

**Traditional reading:** Micah (a shortened form of *Micaiah*, meaning "Who is like Jehovah?") hailed from Moresheth-Gath, a village in the lowland of Judah about 25 miles southwest of Jerusalem, near the Philistine border. Like Amos, he was a country man sent to the cities. He prophesied during the overlapping reigns of Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah (c. 739–686 BC), making him a contemporary of Isaiah. The phrase "the word of the LORD…which he saw" indicates that the entire book is divine revelation received through prophetic vision. "Concerning Samaria and Jerusalem" shows he addressed both kingdoms. Samaria is named first because it was riper for judgment and fell first (722 BC to Assyria). ["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm); ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm); ["Enduring Word"](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-1/)

**Reformed (Ligonier):** Notes that when Micah uses "Israel," he typically means the ideal united kingdom, expressing hope that God's people would be reunited. ["Ligonier"](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/word-lord-through-micah)

---

### v. 2 — The Courtroom Summons

**Traditional reading:** Micah opens with a universal summons—"Hear, all ye peoples" (plural)—calling not just Israel but all nations and the earth itself as witnesses. This is a covenant lawsuit scene: the Lord God is both witness and judge. "From his holy temple" means from heaven (cf. Psalm 11:4). The threefold "Hear ye" (1:2; 3:1; 6:1) marks the three major divisions of the book. Micah deliberately echoes Micaiah ben Imlah's words in 1 Kings 22:28. ["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm); ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm); ["Utley/StudyLight"](https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ubc/micah-1.html)

---

### v. 3 — The LORD Descends

**Traditional reading:** A grand theophany in figurative language: the LORD "comes forth out of His place" (heaven), roused by Israel's sins. "Will come down" is anthropomorphic (cf. Gen 18:21). "Tread upon the high places" implies God's absolute sovereignty—the very mountains that were sites of idolatrous worship are trampled under His feet. ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm); ["Enduring Word"](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-1/)

**Reformed (Ligonier):** Pictures the Lord coming forth to do battle—normally good news for His people (cf. 2 Chron 32:8; Zech 14), but here Israel and Judah are the enemies of God because of their idolatry. ["Ligonier"](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/word-lord-through-micah)

---

### v. 4 — Creation Undone

**Traditional reading:** The imagery recalls the revelation at Sinai (Exodus 19) and may allude to a memorable earthquake in the days of Uzziah (Amos 1:1). Mountains "melt like wax" (Psalm 97:5) and valleys split open like water poured down a steep place. The mountains—symbols of stability and strength—dissolve before the Judge. The inanimate creation shares in the effects of, and serves as an instrument in, judgment on man. Ellicott quotes Dean Stanley: "Mountains and valleys are cleft asunder, and melt as in a furnace…" ["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm); ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm)

---

### v. 5 — The Cause: Sin Centered in the Capitals

**Traditional reading:** The dramatic divine descent is "all this…for the transgression of Jacob." The corruption radiates from the capital cities: Samaria = the apostasy of the northern kingdom (Baal worship introduced by Ahab); Jerusalem = the "high places" (unauthorized or idolatrous shrines) of Judah. Hezekiah's reforms hadn't yet occurred. ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm); ["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** Applies the principle that "judgment begins at the house of God" (1 Peter 4:17). The people likely saw surrounding pagan nations as more corrupt and thought judgment unfair—but God holds His own people to a higher standard. ["Enduring Word"](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-1/)

---

### vv. 6–7 — Samaria's Destruction

**Traditional reading:** v. 6 — Samaria would be reduced to "a heap of the field" and "plantings of a vineyard"—essentially returning to what it was before Omri bought the hill from Shemer (1 Kings 16:24). This is a standard Assyrian formula for total destruction found in the inscriptions of Tiglath-Pileser. The stones would be hurled down into the valley from the hilly platform on which Samaria stood—a prophecy travelers confirm is literally fulfilled. ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm); ["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm)

v. 7 — Idolatry is spiritual adultery. The "hires" are offerings made to idol temples, likened to a prostitute's wages. The carved images would be smashed; the costly idols plated with precious metals would be burned. The treasures obtained by spiritual harlotry would be carried off to Nineveh to adorn Assyrian temples—"they shall return to the hire of an harlot." Ellicott calls this a proverbial saying akin to *Male parta, male dilabuntur* ("ill-gotten, ill-spent"). ["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm); ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm)

**Reformed (Ligonier):** Emphasizes the irony of God's judgment: Assyria would take the revenue Israel derived from cultic prostitution and use it to pay Assyria's own cultic prostitutes. The judgment fits the crime exactly. ["Ligonier"](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/word-lord-through-micah)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** Quotes Waltke: "Golden images, of such monetary value yet so spiritually and politically worthless, were constructed from the wages of cult prostitutes. The conquerors will break them up and use the money to repeat the same cycle. Only the heart of depraved man could worship gods like that!" ["Enduring Word"](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-1/)

---

### v. 8 — The Prophet's Lament

**Traditional reading:** Micah does not announce judgment dispassionately. "I will wail and howl"—the Hebrew for "wail" means to beat the breast. "Stripped and naked" describes not merely a mourner (who removed outer garments) but a captive stripped for deportation (cf. Isaiah 20:2-4). "Dragons…owls" (KJV) are literally jackals and ostriches, chosen for their mournful, doleful night cries. ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm); ["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** Strong pastoral application: Micah "didn't just announce judgment and then yawn. He cared so deeply that he wept." Quotes Boice: "Many who have rejected a Christian's logic have been won by his tears." ["Enduring Word"](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-1/)

---

### v. 9 — The Wound Reaches Judah

**Traditional reading:** Samaria's "wound" (literally "stripes") is incurable—the day of grace for the northern kingdom has passed. But the same punishment "has come to Judah…to the gate of Jerusalem." "He is come" refers to the enemy (Assyria) as the agent of the "stripe." Ellicott sees the outlying towns shuddering at the invader's advance while Jerusalem itself is spared for now. Pusey thinks Micah refers specifically to Sennacherib's invasion (2 Kings 18:13), though the foreshortened prophetic view may include the final Babylonian ruin. ["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm); ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word):** Applies spiritually: "Our only incurable wounds are the ones we refuse to bring to God. With Him, all things are possible (Luke 18:27), but when we refuse to bring our sin to Him, then our wounds are incurable." ["Enduring Word"](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-1/)

---

### vv. 10–16 — The Lament Over Judah's Towns (Paronomasia Section)

**Traditional reading (general):** These verses form a series of wordplays (*paronomasia*) on the names of towns in the Shephelah (the lowlands between the coastal plain and the Judean hills), tracing the route of the Assyrian invader. The puns are not jesting but reflect the ancient belief that a name expressed character and destiny. Micah shows how each town's name becomes a prophecy of its fate. Compare Isaiah 10:28-32 for a similar description of Sennacherib's advance. ["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm); ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm); ["Enduring Word"](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-1/)

#### v. 10 — Gath and Beth-leaphrah

**Traditional reading:** "Tell it not in Gath" is lifted verbatim from David's lament over Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:20)—it had become proverbial for not letting enemies gloat. Gath was a Philistine city. Some scholars (with LXX support) emend "weep not at all" (*bako al tibeku*) to "in Acco weep not," making a pun on another foreign city. "Beth-leaphrah" means "House of Dust," so: "In Dust-town, roll yourself in the dust" (a sign of mourning). ["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm); ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm); ["Enduring Word"](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-1/)

#### v. 11 — Shaphir, Zaanan, Beth-ezel

- **Shaphir** ("Beautiful/Fair"): "Depart in shameful nakedness, O dwellers of Fair-town"—go from beauty into foul dishonour.
- **Zaanan** ("Going forth/Exit"): The dwellers of "Exit-town" will not come forth at all—they will be shut up by siege.
- **Beth-ezel** ("House at one's side/Nearby house"): "Neighbour-town" will be no neighbour; its support (or "standing") is taken away. The lamentation of Beth-ezel affords no refuge.

["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm); ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm); ["Enduring Word"](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-1/)

#### v. 12 — Maroth

**Traditional reading:** Maroth means "Bitterness." The inhabitants "pined" (or "writhed in anguish") for good, having lost property or liberty, but instead "calamity came down from the LORD, even to the gate of Jerusalem." The Assyrian invasion reached the very gates of the capital (cf. Isaiah 22:7; 36:2). ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm); ["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm)

#### v. 13 — Lachish

**Traditional reading:** Lachish was the most important of the cities listed—a major fortress city fortified by Rehoboam, later captured by Sennacherib after a long siege (a bas-relief of this conquest is in the British Museum). The name sounds like *larekkesh* ("to the horses/steeds"), so: "Inhabitant of Horse-town, harness your horses [to flee]!" Lachish is called "the beginning of sin to the Daughter of Zion" because, as a border city, it was the channel through which the idolatry of Jeroboam's northern kingdom was introduced into Judah. ["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm); ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm); ["Enduring Word"](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-1/)

#### v. 14 — Moresheth-gath and Achzib

**Traditional reading:** Moresheth (Micah's own hometown) sounds like *meorasah* ("betrothed"). "Give farewell gifts" (or "parting presents") refers either to a dowry sent with a bride or more likely a bill of divorce—the city passes from the "husband" (Judah) to a new possessor (the invader). Achzib means "deceptive" or "disappointing" (like a river that dries up, cf. Jeremiah 15:18). Its houses will be "a lie" (Hebrew *achzab*) to the kings of Israel—a broken reed. ["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm); ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm); ["Enduring Word"](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-1/)

#### v. 15 — Mareshah and Adullam

**Traditional reading:** Mareshah is related to *yoresh* ("possessor" or "heir"), so God will "bring a conqueror" (literally "the possessor" or "heir"—identified by Ellicott as Sennacherib) against "Possessor-town." Mareshah was fortified by Rehoboam and was the scene of Asa's victory over Zerah the Ethiopian. Adullam was David's refuge when fleeing Saul; now "the glory of Israel" (her nobles and leaders) will again flee to Adullam—but this time they will be seized there by the invader. ["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm); ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm); ["Enduring Word"](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-1/)

#### v. 16 — Mourning for the Exiled Children

**Traditional reading:** A call to deep mourning—shaving the head was a common Eastern grief rite, distinct from the idolatrous hair-cutting condemned in Leviticus 19:27-28. "Make yourselves as bald as an eagle" refers to the vulture (the Hebrew *nesher* includes vultures), whose head is entirely bald. "For they will go from you into exile"—Ellicott and Pulpit agree the language of total desolation fits the Babylonian captivity (586 BC) better than Sennacherib's invasion, showing Micah's prophetic foreshortening. ["Ellicott"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/micah/1.htm); ["Pulpit"](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/micah/1.htm)

## Traditions — Where They Differ

**Reformed (Ligonier):** Stresses that all sin is rooted in false worship (citing Romans 1:18-32). The ethical breaches Micah denounces (oppression of the poor, perversion of justice) flow from idolatry. The coram Deo application: "recognizing the idols and false worship behind our other sins advances our sanctification." Judgment on impenitent idolaters is certain. ["Ligonier"](https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/word-lord-through-micah)

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word, David Guzik):** Emphasizes the emotional engagement of the prophet and its application for preachers today. The commentary highlights pastoral warmth—Micah wept, and preachers must do more than announce judgment; they must care. The interpretive lens is strongly applicational: "our character becomes our future." ["Enduring Word"](https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/micah-1/)

**Reformed Baptist (Desiring God / John Piper):** Piper's treatment of Micah 1, though brief (within a sermon on Micah 5), emphasizes the historical reality: Samaria's judgment fell in 722 BC; Jerusalem's exile came in 586 BC. "Micah didn't destroy the nation. They destroyed themselves with idolatry, covetousness, and perverted justice." Piper stresses God's sovereign ordination of judgment through historical events and holds together doom and hope. ["Desiring God"](https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/from-bethlehem-in-the-majesty-of-the-name-of-the-lord)

---

## Gaps

I was unable to access or find specific material from the following traditions for Micah 1:
- **Baptist (Spurgeon, GTY/MacArthur):** No dedicated verse-by-verse treatment of Micah 1 found on the restricted sites.
- **Methodist/Wesleyan (Seedbed, Wesley Center):** No Micah 1 commentary located within search and fetch limits.
- **Lutheran (LCMS, 1517.org):** Not reached within limits.
- **Catholic (newadvent.org, catholic.com) and Orthodox (oca.org):** Not reached.
- **Modern scholarship (bibleodyssey.org, netbible.org):** Not reached—NET Bible notes would have been valuable for textual and translation issues in vv. 10–15 especially.
- **Debated modern movements (prosperity, word of faith, hyper-grace):** No distinctive readings of Micah 1 surfaced from these traditions on the permitted sites.
